doc.title: John Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

chapter: Chicago and the Stuff Smith trio
title: Drifting into the business side: post office job and the Chicago union
summary: Levy studied violin, took up bass with Milt Hinton's help, and learned the union system; the Local 208 president asks him to handle business for Stuff Smith.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Tell us how you moved from — you’re a musician yourself.

Yeah. Well my story is all accidental I call it. I guess I was the type of person who was always interested in the business end of music, right from the very beginning. And I got into it sort of like, as I say accidental, because I had studied violin and then I sort of picked up bass, and Milt Hinton had sort of, we were in school together and Milt had sort of helped me develop that instrument. And I was actually working in the post office and just gigging on the side, because I got married very young so I had a family. And music I didn’t figure was going to be the thing for me to —
Don’t quit your day gig, right?

Yeah, that’s the thing. Yeah that’s something else. So we spent a lot of time, you know, learning about the inside of the business. For example at that time the musicians’ union was very strong so you had to, in each city you went to play you had to report to the union and so I learned all about that part of the business. And by accident, here again I use the word accident, I was working in the post office and the president of the musicians’ union, the Local 208 which was the black local in Chicago at the time, we’re talking about all this happening in Chicago during that period. And he called me in and he said, “I’ve got a guy here, Stuff Smith, and we’ll let him work in this city, but only if somebody like you can take charge and collect the money and handle the business,” he says, “because Stuff is not reliable. He’s a great jazz violinist and all that, but he’s not a very reliable person.” So I said, “fine.” So I met Stuff and there was Raymond Walters was the piano player that had been chosen to work with Stuff. It was just a trio — violin, piano and bass. So we had this engagement downtown and they told me that there was an agent who booked Stuff, and his name was Joe Glaser, and that he was the booking person who was doing it but he couldn’t come in to Chicago because they had a rap against him, or some kind of rap, because he’d been involved with gangsters. So —
